pr_title: ENH: add fold support to Timestamp constructor
pr_body:
**PERF Note:** Current implementation slows down the `Timestamp` constructor. I've tested this thoroughly and tracked it down to ba7fcd5 where I changed the function signatures at the very beginning of working on the PR. The performance overhead appeared before any of the logic was implemented.

- [X] closes #25057, closes #31338 
- [X] tests added 32 / passed 32
- [X] passes `black pandas`
- [X] passes `git diff upstream/master -u -- "*.py" | flake8 --diff`
- [X] whatsnew entry

### Reasoning for changes
We currently don't support fold from [PEP 495](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0495/#the-fold-attribute), and this causes us a lot of grief, including, but not limited to, broken Timestamp representations at the edge of DST shift (see #31338). The values can also break.

Support of the fold attribute helps us deal with that. Now, if the wall clock time occurs twice due to a DST shift, we will know exactly at which point in time we are.

This also removes inconsistencies between using `pytz` and `dateutil`: now both the values and representations match for both timezone packages near DST summer/winter shifts.

### Scope of PR
Implementing fold into Timestamp can easily get out of hand. Parent `pydatetime` has it easy, as the object doesn't need to sync its underlying epoch time, fold, and the representation, like we do.

This PR is already large, so I propose we limit its scope to minimal consistent fold support:
- when fold is explicitly supplied, attempt to shift value across the DST boundary according to the value supplied
- infer fold from value during tz-aware Timestamp construction. For example, if Timestamp is built from epoch time, then we can infer fold.
- pass the resulting fold to the underlying `datetime` constructor in `create_timestamp_from_ts` so that it gets stored in the object (can't assign it directly as it's read-only).
- implement local timezone support for fold. Don't have any idea how to do this though.

Things I suggest we leave to discussion and other PRs:
- conflicts resolution. A user can supply `fold=1` for a datetime that is nowhere near a DST shift. We can raise and Error or a Warning in the future. For now, we check whether `fold` can be 1, and if not, we leave it as default `fold=0`.
- consider reintroducing ambiguous time errors. Currently, the implementation assumes `fold == 0` for ambiguous time like Timestamp("2019-10-27 01:30:00", tz='Europe/London'). The error was dropped to mirror the `fold=0` default in pydatetime and to allow the fold attribute to be `bint` in Cython functions.

**Note:** `pydatetime` doesn't infer fold from value and doesn't raise errors when you assign `fold=1` nowhere near a fold. Example:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from dateutil.tz import gettz

dt = datetime.datetime(2015, 10, 27, 5, 30, 0, 0, gettz("Europe/London"), fold=1)
dt.fold
OUT:
1
```

### Performance problems
This implementation behaves as I expect it to, but it slows down scalar constructor benchmarks by 30-70%, even for tz-naive benchmarks.

Update: since the benchmark slowdown appeared before any of the functionality, this has nothing to do with the logic introduced and all to do with adding `bint fold` to function signatures, apparently. I'm afraid I don't know Cython well enough to research further.

### General notes on the method used
The PR focuses on inferring fold from `Timestamp.value` and adjusting `Timestamp.value` for the fold constructor argument, and this can be done if we have DST transition times and offsets, which we get out of both pytz and dateutil with `get_dst_info`. Then we take the nearest transition point, the DST delta, and the `Timestamp.value`, and this is enough to either infer `Timestamp.fold` or adjust `Timestamp.value` for fold supplied during construction.

@pganssle (and @jreback and @mroeschke to join the discussion)

Thank you for the detailed comments. I know how much time it takes to dig through the Timestamp constructor implementation, and I sympathize.
I will try to set aside the resources I've already invested in this PR. Let's discuss our options.

If I understand your comments correctly, your primary gripe is not so much with this PR as it is with the way Timestamp tz-aware construction is handled in general. I think so, because we don't handle it the way you suggest in your first comment. I don't like the general tz-aware construction approach either and would have preferred to implement fold support into something more transparent.

My approach was to limit the scope of this PR to implementing fold into the current structure while changing as little code as possible and getting desired behavior. To this end, I added the value-fold syncing code near to where we were already converting `dts` to `value` and back. I think the only place I relied on the implementation of pytz and dateutil was using `get_dst_info` which builds dst transition points and deltas out of library-specific information. There is no code written specifically for one of the libraries.

While we do have some disagreements on what desired fold behavior is and in which cases we should raise, this is secondary and should be dealt with later.

What we should **all** decide upon first is the general approach. From what I see, we have three options here, but I'd be happy to have missed something:

1. Accept the approach currently taken in this PR, tweak the desired behavior to something we can all accept, and move on. This will reduce the transparency of the code a bit, and we'll be compounding our existing reliance on `get_dst_info`.
2. First refactor the way tz-aware Timestamps are built, according to the logic suggested by @pganssle, and only then implement fold. This way we'll end up with the cleanest code, but it will take the most effort. The probability of introducing bugs is difficult to predict.
3. Build Timestamp like we used to, and then try to sync up `Timestamp.value` and `Timestamp.fold`. This option is crutchy, and I don't like it, but it's available.

@pganssle, sorry for not addressing all your comments, but I believe that would be wasting everyone's time until we decide if the current implementation should be thrown out.

P.S. To be transparent: I'm not volunteering to make another implementation if we discard this one.

2) is a non-starter; we have had this construction and conversion method since the very beginning. changing would be an enormous effort with little gain and a non trivial chance of adding bugs (even though we have a large test suite). @pganssle thr approach is what it is; you may not like it or even fully understand it but we are not going to radically change it

I do think a radical restructuring is a good idea, because *way* more effort is spent maintaining relatively slow and creaky timezone code than would be required to maintain a separate time zone implementation, but that's not really what I've suggested here.

I actually don't really understand what options 1, 2 and 3 would look like in your conception, because I haven't really proposed any fundamental changes to how timestamps are created here, I've just pointed out multiple places where you've introduced redundant degrees of freedom / unnecessary arguments, and where you've apparently unnecessarily introduced fold-handling logic. I think it would be better to just respond to my individual suggestions so we can get on the same page as to what the radical restructuring you're talking about is.

> I have to admit I'm a bit puzzled about your comment on pytz not supporting fold. There is currently no pytz-specific code in the fold implementation in this PR, and everything works the same for pytz and dateutil: value, fold, and offset all match.
> Am I missing a test case?

You've actually *removed* a test case where `pytz` behaves differently from `dateutil`, [this one](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/31563#discussion_r377180214). `pytz` defines its own non-standard semantics and doesn't use `fold`. That makes this a breaking change for anyone who relies on `pytz`'s existing semantics. You must have backported the logic unintentionally, because `pytz` simply ignores `fold`.

> You've actually _removed_ a test case where `pytz` behaves differently from `dateutil`, [this one](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/31563#discussion_r377180214). `pytz` defines its own non-standard semantics and doesn't use `fold`. That makes this a breaking change for anyone who relies on `pytz`'s existing semantics. You must have backported the logic unintentionally, because `pytz` simply ignores `fold`.

Copying my comment in reply to the test removal.
_____
Not really. What I'm doing is setting fold to 0 by default for Timestamp construction from ambiguous times. I based this decision on the behavior of pydatetime, which doesn't raise an error and just sets fold to 0.
```python
from datetime import datetime
from pytz import timezone

tz = timezone('Europe/London')
dt = datetime(2019, 10, 27, 1, 30, 0, 0, tzinfo=tz)
dt.fold
OUT:
0
```
I also propose we consider reintroducing the error on ambiguous time construction later.
_____
Adding to the former comment: the reason this removes the pytz error is that `fold=0` propagates all the way to `tz_localize_to_utc`, where it sets the `ambiguous` argument. This lets `tz_localize_to_utc` resolve the ambiguity according to the default.

I would appreciate any other cases, since this is behaving in accordance with the proposed default.

The reason why I think what you propose is quite different from the current algorithm is this bit:

> * Convert `ts` to whatever time zone you need it to be in so that the civil time is correct.
> * Convert `ts` to `numpy.datetime64`, ignoring `fold` and `tzinfo`
> * Set `obj.fold` and `obj.tzinfo` to their respective values on `ts`
> * Call `ts.timestamp()` or convert to UTC then subtract off the epoch time, then adjust with any smaller components you need like nanoseconds, set that to `value`.

To me, this looks quite different from the current implementation. For example, this is what we do when building from datetime right now, as far as I understand.

* Convert `ts` to the new timezone
* Convert `ts` to `numpy.datetime64`, ignoring `fold` and `tzinfo` (so far so good)
* Set obj.value to `ts` scaled to nanoseconds, build obj.dts from ts.
* Set obj.tzinfo to `tz`
* Adjust obj.value for utc_offset to make sure that at one moment in time different timezones share obj.value across the globe.
* Add nanoseconds

After this is where we end up with the bugs this PR is attempting to solve, so I propose introducing two extra steps:

* Adjust obj.value for fold if possible
* Infer fold from the object to make sure that we don't end up with `fold==1` nowhere near a DST shift.

The reason why I think the alternative approach would require some major refactoring is because we don't always have something to call `timestamp()` on. For example when we build from `int` and use `localize_tso`. I believe this is the reason for the approach taken: it lets us process different types of inputs to the constructor similarly instead of relying on `pydatetime` functionality only where its available.

And our own `timestamp` method relies on `obj.value`, so we can't use it to set obj.value:
```python
    def timestamp(self):
        """Return POSIX timestamp as float."""
        # GH 17329
        # Note: Naive timestamps will not match datetime.stdlib
        return round(self.value / 1e9, 6)
```

> To me, this looks quite different from the current implementation. For example, this is what we do when building from datetime right now, as far as I understand.

Yes, it is a simpler implementation that allows you to abstract away many unnecessary details, but it's not fundamentally different in what it *does*, because AFAICT it maintains all guaranteed properties of the existing function. The "call `.timestamp()` on `ts` to get `value`" part of my proposed implementation is actually does all the remaining steps *for you*.

It's possible that this logic was moved into `pandas` deliberately for some reason like speed, but I'd like to see a benchmark or something before rejecting what is essentially a beneficial refactoring of the code on the grounds that it is different than the code that hopefully does exactly the same thing.

> And our own `timestamp` method relies on `obj.value`, so we can't use it to set obj.value:

I don't think that this is a major problem, because the function we're talking about takes what I have to assume is a *valid* `timestamp` (which may be a `datetime`), and converts it to a new `timestamp`, so `ts.timestamp()` should always give the right answer, even when `obj.timestamp()` wouldn't, because `obj.timestamp()` is in an invalid state.

Even if you did have a partially-initialized `obj` and you wanted to convert it to a timestamp, that's not insurmountable by any means. It's basically what `super()` is for, and you can re-create that with `obj.value = datetime.timestamp(obj)`.

--

One last thing to note about this: regardless of whether my proposed simplification of the logic in that one function is desirable, taking `fold` in that function still makes it over-specified. Since `fold` is already an attribute of `ts`, you are effectively taking the `fold` argument twice, which is unnecessary.

Thanks for noticing the unexpected raise for a naive datetime. Changed the raise behavior to accomodate such cases.

`obj` is of type `_TSObject` which is a barebones Cython extension type and doesn't inherit from anything, so it's not possible to call `timestamp` at that point. This means that if we want to rely on `timestamp()` we have to either build a datetime object or have one supplied as an argument.

The reason why `fold` is passed explicitly around instead of being stored in obj.fold from the start is that this allows us to set obj.fold to 0 and then infer the correct value when we are done. In my opinion, it makes code more transparent, but it's a matter of opinion.

We could write fold to `obj.fold` at the beginning of `convert_to_tsobject` and then rely on that. I just like it more to set it to 0 and changing it to 1 only when we are confident.

> `obj` is of type `_TSObject` which is a barebones Cython extension type and doesn't inherit from anything, so it's not possible to call `timestamp` at that point. This means that if we want to rely on `timestamp()` we have to either build a datetime object or have one supplied as an argument.

I think you are misunderstanding what I am suggesting here. There are two major places where I remember that this is an issue:

1. In [`convert_datetime_to_tso`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/31563/files#r377163395), you already have an existing object that includes fold information. It's either a `datetime` (or `datetime` subclass), or it's a `Timestamp` object. You don't need to pass in a `fold` attribute because you can pull it from the `ts` argument. I *also* believe that you don't need that information *anyway*, but if you decide to otherwise leave this function alone completely, you should drop the `fold` argument entirely and in the first line set `fold = ts.fold` or `fold = getattr(ts, "fold", 0)`.

2. In [`localize_tso`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/31563/files#r377170627), the docstring says "Given the UTC nanosecond timestamp in obj.value, find the wall-clock representation of that timestamp in the given timezone.". The contract of the function explicitly states that `obj.value` must be valid, and `obj.value` is *always unambiguous*. The job of `localize_tso` is to find all the components of the local datetime that correspond to `value`. One of those components is `fold`.

  Taking `fold` as an argument to `localize_tso` makes no more sense than taking `year` or `day`: that information all needs to be calculated from `obj.value`.

As for the question of when you can rely on `.timestamp()`, in `convert_datetime_to_tso`, you *explicitly take a `datetime` or `Timestamp` object*, so you can rely on its contents and methods to populate your new `Timestamp` object. You can calculate `value()` from `ts.timestamp()` not `obj.timestamp()`.

In `localize_tso` I am not suggesting using `timestamp()`, though there are other options like `.fromtimestamp()`. Either way, by default you should rely on the time zone providers to use and set fold, and not attempt to do it yourself.

**updated localize_tso docstring to reflect fold treatment behavior**

@pganssle
Fold is a pretty obscure parameter, so my approach is to override instead of raise if at all possible. I assume that if a user gets to setting fold in the constructor, they know what they are doing, and we should attempt to set fold to what they supplied. For tz-aware datetime, it makes sense to raise to me, because the user can just run `dt.replace(fold=x)` before passing `dt` to our constructor. For other types of unambiguous input, I chose to let the user override if they want to, so they don't have to mess with strings, integers, etc. I think this reasoning and the rarity of the use case justify this behavior.

I agree with you in principle that it would be better if pandas left messing with date and timezone internals, posix timetamps, etc. to specialized packages. But we do mess with them, and I think we've established we won't change that in this PR.

If we accept this assumption, then the fold processing in `localize_tso` makes sense, simply because we don't have the variables necessary to make the adjustments and to infer while in `convert_to_tsobject` where it's called from. Pulling everything we need into that function would be worse. I've updated the `localize_tso` docstring to make things more clear.

In the future, somebody can attempt to refactor the Timestamp constructor for tz-aware cases in another PR, carefully benchmark alternatives, test everything, and try to convince us the risks such refactoring would introduce are as mitigated as possible and worth it. I might even try it myself in a month or too. But I just don't see why we must attempt it now.

I think, at this point, we have both stated our positions and reasoning very clearly, and there are no more misunderstandings. If neither of us can convince the other, let's just wait for other reviewers to weigh in and go from there (@jreback @mroeschke). I don't think that keeping going will accomplish much except increase the discussion word-count.

I agree with @pganssle sentiment in general that we should rely on the underlying `datetime.datetime` (or subclass `Timestamp`) + dateutil's handling of `fold` instead of trying to pass it around (I was initially very surprised with the amount of code we needed to add just to incorporate `fold`).

Though I'll admit, I haven't fully studied this PR's change (or the change necessary in general) to adequately support `fold` in the `Timestamp` constructor

I agree with the general sentiment too--that's not the problem. It's just that implementing fold in accordance with that sentiment, in my opinion, clashes with how we currently do things and must involve refactoring the functions in `conversion.pyx` to implement it right. Otherwise we'll end up with a hybrid that partially outsorces stuff and partially does things itself, and it isn't good.
 
But obviously I'm biased in favor of my current solution and also frustrated with this PR in general, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

> Fold is a pretty obscure parameter, so my approach is to override instead of raise if at all possible. I assume that if a user gets to setting fold in the constructor, they know what they are doing, and we should attempt to set fold to what they supplied

Fold is *not* an "obscure parameter", it is a *component of the datetime*, just like `day` or `microsecond`. In time zones with ambiguous datetimes, it is required to fully specify the point on the timeline. It should be treated essentially exactly like those other parameters (which is again why it should not be passed to `convert_datetime_to_tso` or `localize_tso`).

That said, apparently the semantics of `Timestamp` are a bit... strange:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp(datetime(2019, 1, 4), year=2025, month=12, day=5, hour=5)
Timestamp('2019-01-04 00:00:00')
```

I would 100% expect this to raise, but apparently the behavior of the constructor is to *ignore* individual components passed if a timestamp is also passed. This should *probably* be deprecated in favor of raising an exception IMO, but that can be a separate issue. I still think it would be a good idea to raise if `fold` is passed in a situation where you are not using the by-component constructor, but I think a case could be made for simply doing what is done for all other components and ignore it even if there's a conflict.

> If we accept this assumption, then the fold processing in `localize_tso` makes sense, simply because we don't have the variables necessary to make the adjustments and to infer while in `convert_to_tsobject` where it's called from. Pulling everything we need into that function would be worse. I've updated the `localize_tso` docstring to make things more clear.

Again this is simply not true, unless you are saying the docstring is *currently* inaccurate. Currently, `localize_tso` takes `obj.value` and `tz` as the source of truth. That is enough to find the `fold`.

Again I encourage you to read up on this issue a bit more thoroughly if you want to make the case for doing something else. Some resources:

- [My talk at PyCon 2019 on time zones](https://ganssle.io/talks/#working-with-timezones-pycon) (link has links to slides, video and repo)
- [My blog post on the subject](https://blog.ganssle.io/articles/2018/03/pytz-fastest-footgun.html)
- [PEP 495](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0495/)

Fold is almost always 0. Year is not. Year is also not set by default if you have month and day. Desired behavior and argument treatment can differ dependent on the rarity of the use case and the acceptability of defaults.

<s>We don't necessarily arrive in `localize_tso` with a valid `obj.value`. To set it correctly, we need information that is available in `localize_tso` and isn't available in `convert_to_tsobject`. We need to refactor both functions if we want to be sure that we have a valid `obj.value` when we call `localize_tso`.</s> fold is passed to `localize_tso` to allow overriding as established below.

Again, this isn't getting us anywhere. I have familiarized myself with PEP 495 and with your blog post before and during working on this PR. I truly think that we both have all the information here, so further clarifications don't help. We just don't agree on what approaches are acceptable in the scope of this PR.

> We don't necessarily arrive in `localize_tso` with a valid `obj.value`.

This is simply not true, the docstring of `localize_tso` *specifically says* that it is for adjusting `obj.dts` and `obj.tzinfo` *holding `obj.value` constant*. It is only your changes to the interface that are fundamentally changing the way the function works, presumably as an expedient for your implementation of `convert_datetime_to_tso`.

You are right. We end up in `localize_tso` if we build from `int`, let's say. The only reason `fold` is passed into `localize_tso` is to allow the user to override with a `fold` value that doesn't match the epoch time if it's possible.

Apologies for the misunderstanding.

Clarification: `localize_tso` doesn't have much to do with `datetime_to_tsobject`. The first is called when we create from int, the second, when we create from datetime or str. It's definitely not a case of two mistakes cancelling each other, but I need a moment to research.

I think probably "completely ignore fold unless using the datetime-like constructor" is a reasonably defensible position.

It might be reasonable to allow setting `fold` when `ts_input` is naive and `tz` or `tzinfo` is specified in `Timestamp`, but that can get a bit messy because `datetime.fold` has no "unset" value, and it would be the reverse of all the other individual components in that the value passed to the `Timestamp` component is overriding the value in the `datetime` component.

Also, `fold` should have no effect on `pytz` zones, and it seems like most people are going to use `pytz` because of `pandas`' unfortunate default.

The "parsing a naive string" case is trickier, because there's an argument to be made that the string is actually just another representation of the individual components, but there's no acceptable string representation for `fold`, so it might make sense to allow `fold` to be passed there. I am basically indifferent for that one.

One thing I'll note is that probably most people who are parsing arbitrary naive strings (rather than string literals) will actually want an argument like `default_fold_for_ambiguous` rather than `fold` itself, since there *is* no `fold`. The semantics of `fold` make it so that you can treat it as if it means `default_fold_if_ambiguous`, because PEP 495 says that `fold` must be ignored outside of ambiguous and imaginary times, but conceptually it may change the preferred semantics to consider that a `Timestamp` constructed with `fold` meaning "default to STD instead of DST" probably should retain an artifact of how it was constructed even when it is semantically identical to another unambiguous `Timestamp` (i.e. the object's `fold` will be set to 1).

@pganssle 
Thank you.

I don't want to leave the repo with unintuitive behavior after this PR, so I propose some adjustments, mainly to raise and not silently ignore (until all raising behavior is brought into sync in another PR, possibly one that solves #31930).

Use cases:
1. We build from number-like (int, float, np.datetime64). Raise if float is passed along with arguments of these types. You will be able to refactor this in #31930, especially if we decide to remove the option of timezone-aware Timestamp building from value as @mroeschke suggests. But even if not, there will be room to change error-raising behavior. For now, we won't be leaving the user hanging without an error or a warning to understand what they did wrong.
2. We build from datetime-like. Raise if it's not naive and fold is passed.
3. We build from string. Raise if fold is passed. I see no easy way to check if string represents an ambiguous or unambiguous time (please point out if you know one). `parse_iso_8601_datetime` in `np_datetime_strings.c`  does this properly and it requires parsing the whole string.
4. We build from components. No need to raise.

When parsing from potentially ambiguous input without fold specified, I propose we set fold to 1 (standard time) by default and don't raise.

We also guarantee that after the object is built, `fold`, `value` and offsets all match, both for `pytz` and `dateutil`. This is about the fact that if the user passes `fold` with a timezone with DST transitions, it's on us ot make sure that nanoseconds since EPOCH correspond to the correct side of the DST transition (this will also ensure that `Timestamp.timestamp()` works correctly). We can accomplish this with the proposed `_adjust_tsobject_for_fold` function with some minor tweaks. For unambiguous time, there would be no harm if `fold` didn't match `value`, since it wouldn't be relevant as per PEP 495. But since we guarantee for ambiguous time (and we don't know if it's ambiguous in advance), there is no additional cost to also make sure that `fold == 0` for unambiguous time, and the object can't represent an invalid time in this regard. 

This behavior will also make it so that `localize_tso` doesn't need to adjust `obj.value`, and, in general, passing fold around will be avoidable. 

Would this be an acceptable solution?
I'll proceed with this approach then.

> I don't want to leave the repo with unintuitive behavior after this PR, so I propose some adjustments, mainly to raise and not silently ignore (until all raising behavior is brought into sync in another PR, possibly one that solves #31930).

I'm more or less fine with this approach, but there are a few points speaking against it:

1. It is somewhat unintuitive to me that `fold` is treated differently than other datetime components, which are ignored as reported in #31930. It makes sense to have them all do the same thing.
2. Whether or not this is a breaking change depends on how you define "breaking". We do not have a "clean slate" right now because `Timestamp` already accepts the `fold` argument, it simply *ignores* it, in all cases. An argument could be made that starting to raise an exception when it's passed in some cases is a breaking change (even if a desirable one), and one that should go through a deprecation cycle.

I don't know what pandas considers a breaking change or not, so I will leave it up to @jreback and @mroeschke to decide that. I do think the end goal should involve `fold` raising when passed with any unambiguous datetime.

> When parsing from potentially ambiguous input without fold specified, I propose we set fold to 1 (standard time) by default and don't raise.

Strong disagreement here. PEP 495 says that `fold` defaults to 0, we should respect that.

> We also guarantee that after the object is built, `fold`, `value` and offsets all match, both for `pytz` and `dateutil`. This is about the fact that if the user passes `fold` with a timezone with DST transitions, it's on us to make sure that nanoseconds since EPOCH correspond to the correct side of the DST transition (this will also ensure that `Timestamp.timestamp()` works correctly)

This I don't understand. You can totally discard nanoseconds because it's not even possible for `dateutil` or `pytz` time zones to support time zone transitions that occur between two microseconds. If a datetime truncated to the nearest microsecond has a given offset, the datetime has the same offset. It is sufficient to know the value of `nanos` and the correct value of `value` to microsecond precision.

@pganssle 
Sorry about the nanoseconds phrase. Bad choice of words: what I meant was total time since EPOCH in nanoseconds.
I've also realized there is no reason to set the default to 1. Misread something way back in the discussion, I'm afraid.
The current version, I believe, addresses most of your concerns. Pinging everyone in the next post, please tell me if you find this version more acceptable.

@jreback @mroeschke @pganssle
Did my best to address @pganssle's concerns, and I think this PR is ready to be reviewed again.

Changes in behavior and implementation:
1. We adjust `Timestamp.value` for `fold` only if `ts_input` is naive datetime-like or if we build from components. If the input is unambiguous (or can be unambiguous as when we build from string), we raise a ValueError if fold is supplied too. Basically, on conflicts we raise, and this also eliminates changing `obj.value` unless we are building from naive datetime-like or components. Both @mroeschke and @pganssle suggested this, and I think it's the safest approach until we refactor.
2. `fold` isn't passed beyond `convert_to_tsobject` anymore. We use `obj.fold` where necessary as @pganssle suggested.
3. `pytz.AmbiguousTimeError` is back when we try to build from an ambiguous string like `2019-10-27 01:30:00` with `pytz`. This is a natural consequence of not messing with `obj.value` unless we are building from naive datetime-like.

Notes:
If we build from components, default `fold` is 0. This fits PEP 495 suggestion for default in the constructor, and there is no reason to prefer DST to standard or vice-versa anyway.

Thanks to @pganssle's explanation, I have finally found how we manage to get different offsets for different sides of fold when buildling with the pytz timezone. It's a completely separate mechanism from fold support:
```python
        elif typ in ['pytz', 'dateutil']:
            pos = trans.searchsorted(obj.value, side='right') - 1
```

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

If we make a Timestamp in an ambiguous DST period while specifying via the offset (or by supplying `Timestamp.value` directly) that the time is before DST switch, the representation then shows that this is after DST switch. This is backed up by calling `Timestamp.tz.utcoffset(Timestamp)`.

```python

IN:
t1 = pd.Timestamp(1382837400000000000, tz='dateutil/Europe/London')
t1

OUT:
Timestamp('2013-10-27 01:30:00+0100', tz='dateutil/GB-Eire')

IN:
t2 = pd.Timestamp(1382837400000000000, tz='Europe/London')
t2

OUT:
Timestamp('2013-10-27 01:30:00+0000', tz='Europe/London')
```


#### Problem description


The reason for this bug looks to be buried deep in the interaction of `pandas` and `dateutil`.

So this is what I've been able to dig up. When we try to determine whether we are in DST or not, we rely on `timezone.utcoffset` of the underlying timezone package. What gets executed in `dateutil` is this:

```python
def utcoffset(self, dt):
	...

	return self._find_ttinfo(dt).delta
	
def _find_ttinfo(self, dt):
	idx = self._resolve_ambiguous_time(dt)
	...

def _resolve_ambiguous_time(self, dt):
	idx = self._find_last_transition(dt)

	# If we have no transitions, return the index
	_fold = self._fold(dt)
	if idx is None or idx == 0:
		return idx

	# If it's ambiguous and we're in a fold, shift to a different index.
	idx_offset = int(not _fold and self.is_ambiguous(dt, idx))

	return idx - idx_offset
```

`dateutil` is expecting an ordinary `datetime.timedelta` object here, so this is what it does:

1. Use `_find_last_transition` to get the index of the last DST transition before `dt`. This is done by computing `timedelta.total_seconds` since epoch time. Our `pandas.Timedelta.total_seconds` is smart, and returns different `total_seconds` for before and after `DST`, since we basically return `Timedelta.value` which is the same as `Timestamp.value` when counting since epoch time (because of how `_Timestamp.__sub__` in `c_timestamp.pyx` is implemented).

This is what we do (doesn't care about `dt.replace(tzinfo=None)`):
```python
def total_seconds(self):
	"""
	Total duration of timedelta in seconds (to microsecond precision).
	"""
	# GH 31043
	# Microseconds precision to avoid confusing tzinfo.utcoffset
	return (self.value - self.value % 1000) / 1e9
```
This is what `datetime.timedelta` does (loses DST awareness after `dt.replace(tzinfo=None)`):
```python
def total_seconds(self):
	"""Total seconds in the duration."""
	return ((self.days * 86400 + self.seconds) * 10**6 +
			self.microseconds) / 10**6
```
2. The remainder of `_resolve_ambiguous_time` corrects for ambiguous times, since `datetime.timedelta.total_seconds` after `dt.replace(tzinfo=None)` isn't DST-aware. It checks if we are in an ambiguous period and if this is the first time this time has occured: this is what `self._fold` is for. [fold](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0495/#the-fold-attribute) is 0 for the first time, and 1 for the second time. If it's the first time, `dateutil` shifts the relevant transition index back by 1, since it thinks that `total_seconds` always returns the number of seconds calculated using the second time.

I'd like to discuss how we are going to approach this. From what I see, there isn't much we can do on our end. ~Making `total_seconds` non-DST-aware by default is bad, because that would be making our implementation less precise unless the user passes a parameter.~ Scratch that. The problem isn't so much the `total_seconds` implementation as it is the `Timestamp.__sub__` implementation which preserves `value` when we subtract epoch time.

Another approach is to go to `dateutil` with this and implement a check there to avoid running the correction if they are dealing with a `pandas.Timedelta`. Might be tricky to do without introducing a dependency on pandas, though.

First came across this while solving #24329 in #30995 

#### Expected Output
```python
IN:
t1
OUT:
Timestamp('2013-10-27 01:30:00+0000', tz='dateutil/GB-Eire')
```

comments:
other options
- dateutil expose another method
- move utcoffset computation go pandas (calling private functions if needed)

dateutil could also expose a setting to signal if `total_seconds` of the timedelta implementation it's working with is DST-aware or not, and we could set it on our end. A number of ways this can be done, some less bad than others.

Just in case it's useful.

The reason that correction in `_resolve_ambiguous_time` is necessary is because `dateutil` replaces `tzinfo` of the datetime with `None` before calculating `total_seconds`. This makes the `datetime.timedelta` calculation ignore the `fold` parameter. So the time is assumed to be non-DST (after the shift). Maybe something could be done at that stage (without bouncing calls between `datetime.__sub__` and `tzinfo.utcoffset`). I'll look into it further to see if I get any ideas.

I don't think you've quite diagnosed the problem correctly.  It is true that pandas apparently uses non-standard [datetime arithmetic semantics](https://blog.ganssle.io/articles/2018/02/aware-datetime-arithmetic.html), which could cause problems, but in this case the issue seems to be that `pandas.Timestamp` does not hold a `fold` attribute for some reason:

```
>>> t1.replace(fold=1)
Timestamp('2013-10-27 01:30:00+0100', tz='dateutil//usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/London')
>>> t1.replace(fold=1).fold
0
>>> t1 = pd.Timestamp(1382837400000000000, tz='dateutil/Europe/London')
>>> t1.fold
0
>>> t1.replace(fold=1)
Timestamp('2013-10-27 01:30:00+0100', tz='dateutil//usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/London')
>>> t1.replace(fold=1).fold
0
```

`pytz` doesn't have this problem because it is old and apparently semi-unmaintained and thus does not support PEP 495, so it uses another mechanism to keep track of ambiguous datetimes. It is expected that if you throw away the `fold` information on a `datetime` that you will have trouble in ambiguous datetimes.

@pganssle 
Thanks. I did some more testing and you are absolutely right:

```python
IN:
EPOCH = datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(0)
t1 = pd.Timestamp(1382833800000000000, tz='dateutil/Europe/London')
t1.value

OUT:
1382833800000000000

IN:
t1.replace(tzinfo=None).value

OUT:
1382837400000000000
```

So we can't tell the difference between the first and the second time an ambiguous time occurs after dropping the tzinfo information.

My hypothesis that `pandas` arithmetic somehow incorporates `fold` into it was wrong, and this is good for us. In theory, once we add fold support to the Timestamp constructor, this bug should be fixed. If so, we can mark this issue as a duplicate for #25057.
I'll see if I can come up with a solution.

@pganssle 
Does dateutil's handling of the problem depend on `Python >= 3.6` then?

@AlexKirko No, dateutil has a backport that returns a datetime subclass with a fold attribute if the normal datetime object doesn't have a fold attribute.

In this case it shouldn't matter much, because Timestamp is itself a datetime subclass, and so the main thing that matters is that it has a meaningful fold attribute.

Thanks, that clears things up.

Started looking into the issue. Caught a cold, but I still hope to have something by the end of the week.

Well, I do have an MVP, but there is still stuff to be done, and I can't seem to find the source of the performance impact that the changes introduce.
If anyone wants to take a look at the PR and help me out, it would be appreciated.

review_comments:
As far as I understand, on master this tests for breakage. Because pytz and dateutil handle fold ambiguity differently, we ended up with different offsets and representations for the same epoch time in what is the same timezone.
With fold support, representatioins, values, and offsets all match.
Does that mean this is a breaking change?

As far as I can tell, no. The test is meaningless right now, because for the same timezone in two packages with the same `tz_localize` call we end up with two different offsets.
I don't know why we are currently testing for the presence of a bug, but this change makes it so that we test for the correct functionality.
